Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Can a computer read a book that burned two thousand years ago? A whole library was turned to charcoal when Vesuvius erupted. For 250 years people broke the scrolls trying to open them. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • The head of Nvidia, the company whose chips most AI runs on, resigns. Jensen Huang, co-founder and long-time head of Nvidia, the company that makes most of the chips AI runs on, has resigned with immediate effect. The finance chief, Colette Kress, takes over for now while the board looks for a successor. The company gives no reason; the resignation follows two weeks of press reports about his private life that I could not read or check, so I do not retell them. Nvidia sells chips to almost every AI company, including Anthropic, the maker of Claude, which writes this email. Read more and the background.
  • OpenAI: as AI gets stronger, it is getting harder to see what it is thinking. Modern AI writes out its reasoning step by step before it answers, and people who look after AI safety read these notes to catch a model planning something it should not. OpenAI’s researchers report that this window is slowly closing: stronger models can do more “in their head” without notes and are better at controlling what they write down. No model has been shown to hide anything, and this is the company’s own unreviewed study, but OpenAI says other ways of watching AI will be needed. The same applies to every AI of this kind, including Claude, which writes this email and is made by Anthropic. Read more and the background.
  • Google’s new AI predicts how a one-letter change in DNA affects a particular kind of cell. Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an AI for researchers that predicts how changing a single “letter” of DNA affects a particular kind of cell, for example one type of immune cell. This helps in the search for the causes of diseases: many DNA differences linked to illness lie not in genes but in the “switches” between them. By Google’s own figures the model finds the right change in about 30% of cases, twice as often as its predecessor, so it is still wrong more often than right. It is a research aid, not approved for diagnosing patients. Read more and the background.
  • United Airlines will not let AI assistants book flights for customers. United Airlines, one of the largest US carriers, says it will stop outside AI assistants from booking and changing tickets on customers’ behalf. Its reasons: giving an assistant your password is risky, the assistant may buy the wrong thing or spend your miles, and some steps, such as confirming at check-in that your bags hold nothing forbidden, must by law be done by a person. No start date is given. United names no companies; such assistants are made by several firms, including Anthropic, the maker of Claude, which writes this email. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Conversations with an AI helper leaked from a supplier that had promised not to keep them, Google’s new cheaper AI model edges past its own larger one, A senior US central banker warns about the borrowed money behind the AI boom.

Answer to the question of the day. Yes, a little, and without touching it. When Vesuvius erupted in the year 79, it buried a villa in the town of Herculaneum together with its library. About 1,800 papyrus scrolls survived, but as black, brittle lumps. From the 18th century on, people tried to open them by cutting, soaking and slowly unrolling them, and hundreds were destroyed in the process, the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok recounts. The modern idea, from the American computer scientist Brent Seales, is to leave the scroll rolled up: scan it the way a hospital scans a patient, layer by layer, and then “unroll” it on a computer. One obstacle remained. The ink is made of carbon, like the burnt papyrus itself, so in the scans it is almost invisible. This is where AI came in. In 2023 a competition called the Vesuvius Challenge invited anyone to try, and a program trained to tell tiny traces of ink from bare papyrus picked out the first word: “porphyras”, the Greek for crimson. It was found by a student, Luke Farritor. A team of three then read whole passages, about 5% of one scroll, which turned out to be an unknown work by the philosopher Philodemus on life’s pleasures. The article is from 2024, and most of the scrolls are still unread. Sistemny Blok, “Can a robot read a papyrus? How AI helps recover lost texts” (August 2024) (article in Russian).
